newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNICEF ties aid to Kabul--let girls go to school.
newsitem.headline: UNICEF ties aid to Kabul--let girls go to school.

text.p: The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said on Tuesday it had put conditions on its latest appeal for Afghanistan -- funds will be raised for education only when the Islamic Taleban allow girls back into schools.
UNICEF is seeking $10.1 million to boost its aid programme for Afghan children and women, whose situation continues to be "among the worst in the world", according to the agency.
It is among a host of U.N. agencies taking part in a $133 million appeal to donor countries launched on Tuesday.

UNICEF's educational aid has been suspended in areas where girls are excluded from attending school since November 1995, two months after Taleban forces seized the main western town of Herat and closed girls' schools.

The policy has been extended to include Kabul, which the Taleban militia captured in September 1996, proclaiming themselves the new rulers of the war-torn country. UNICEF's educational support is limited to the northern region, the area not under Taleban control.
"Although education projects have been included in the appeal, these will only require funding as and when girls are permitted to return to school," UNICEF said in a statement issued in Geneva.
"Girls are prohibited from going to school in two-thirds of the country," it added.
A UNICEF spokeswoman told Reuters: "We are not going to raise funds for areas where education projects are not being undertaken unless the ban is lifted.
"If we can reach boys and girls, we will raise funds and we will go in and do education," she added.
Social services in Afghanistan have been crippled by 17 years of conflict, according to UNICEF.
"The situation for children and women in Afghanistan continues to be among the worst in the world," it said.

The maternal mortality rate of 1,700 per 100,000 live births ranks Afghanistan as the second worst in the world, while the literacy rate for women is probably as low as three to four per cent, according to the agency.
An estimated 249,000 Afghan children aged under five die annually from diarrhoea, measles and respiratory infections.
About $3.1 million of the UNICEF appeal of $10.1 million is earmarked for education, according to a spokeswoman. Of this, about $1.9 million is for areas held by the Taleban.
